result.target_summary: Citigroup's operating expenses decreased 4% to $54.0 billion in 2024, with a 2% decrease to $53.8 billion excluding FDIC special assessments. previous_disclosures.section: Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations > EXECUTIVE SUMMARY > 2023 Results Summary > Expenses
previous_disclosures.summary: Citigroup's 2023 operating expenses totaled $56.4 billion, a 10% increase from the prior year, which included $1.7 billion in FDIC special assessment charges, $780 million in restructuring charges, and $372 million in divestiture-related impacts. Excluding divestiture-related impacts, expenses were $56 billion, and excluding those plus the restructuring and FDIC charges, expenses of $53.5 billion increased 6%, driven by increased investments in risk, controls, technology, severance, and transformation.

materiality_analysis.reason: The disclosure marks a significant reversal in expense trends, moving from a 10% increase in 2023 to a 4% decrease in 2024. It attributes this to organizational simplification savings and notes a new cost driver: a Civil Money Penalty Consent Order with regulators. This changes the narrative from cost expansion to cost management and introduces a new regulatory financial consequence.

comparisons.peer_topic: Noninterest expense increase drivers and prior year comparisons
comparisons.peer_summary: Noninterest expense increased $967 million to $66.8 billion in 2024 compared to 2023, primarily driven by higher revenue-related expenses and investments in people, operations, and technology, partially offset by higher FDIC expense in 2023 (including a $2.1 billion special assessment) and lower expenses from a liquidating business activity.
comparisons.comparison: Citigroup and Bank of America present divergent operating expense trends for 2024 despite both facing FDIC special assessments. Citigroup reported a 4% decrease in operating expenses ($54.0 billion), driven by structural savings and lower prior-year one-offs. Bank of America reported a $967 million increase in noninterest expense ($66.8 billion), driven by higher revenue-related expenses and investments in people/technology. The FDIC assessment impact was a tailwind for both (BAC had $2.1 billion in 2023 vs lower in 2024; C had $1.7 billion in 2023 vs $203 million in 2024), but BAC's core operational growth offset this benefit, whereas Citi's organizational simplification drove a net decline.

sentences.text: Excluding the FDIC special assessment ($203 million in 2024 versus approximately $1.7 billion in the prior year), expenses of $53.8 billion decreased 2%, driven by savings related to Citi's organizational simplification and stranded cost reduction, as well as the lower restructuring charges ($259 million in 2024 versus $781 million in the prior year) and repositioning costs.
Noninterest expense increased $967 million to $66.8 billion in 2024 compared to 2023.

The increase was primarily driven by higher revenue-related expenses as well as investments in people, operations and technology, partially offset by higher Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) expense in 2023, including $2.1 billion for the estimated special assessment amount arising from the closure of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank, and lower expenses related to a liquidating business activity.

comparisons.peer_summary: Operating expenses decreased 2% to $33.77 billion in 2024, aided by lower CIE commercial real estate impairments and prior year one-time charges like the GreenSky write-down, partially offset by higher compensation and transaction expenses, resulting in an efficiency ratio improvement to 63.1% from 74.6%.
comparisons.comparison: Both Citigroup and Goldman Sachs reported a decrease in total operating expenses for 2024, contrasting with Bank of America's increase. However, the primary drivers differed: Citigroup's decrease was driven by organizational simplification savings and lower restructuring charges, while Goldman Sachs' decrease was largely due to lower commercial real estate impairments in CIEs and prior year one-time charges (GreenSky write-down). Both firms cited FDIC special assessments as a factor, but for Goldman Sachs, the prior year had a significant $529 million fee that decreased in 2024, whereas Citigroup had a $203 million assessment in 2024 versus $1.7 billion in 2023. Goldman Sachs also reported an efficiency ratio improvement (63.1% vs 74.6%), a metric not explicitly highlighted for Citigroup in the same summary context.

sentences.text: Excluding the FDIC special assessment ($203 million in 2024 versus approximately $1.7 billion in the prior year), expenses of $53.8 billion decreased 2%, driven by savings related to Citi's organizational simplification and stranded cost reduction, as well as the lower restructuring charges ($259 million in 2024 versus $781 million in the prior year) and repositioning costs.

Operating expenses were $33.77 billion for 2024, 2% lower than 2023, reflecting decreases driven by significantly lower expenses, including impairments, related to commercial real estate in consolidated investment entities (CIEs) and other significant expenses recognized in the prior year, including the write-down of identifiable intangible assets related to GreenSky Holdings, LLC (GreenSky), an impairment of goodwill related to Consumer platforms and the FDIC special assessment fee.

comparisons.peer_topic: Factors driving 2024 operating expense decreases and increases
comparisons.peer_summary: Operating expenses decreased relative to 2023 due to lower commercial real estate impairments, GreenSky intangible asset write-downs, consumer platform goodwill impairments, and FDIC fees, partially offset by higher compensation and transaction-based expenses driven by improved performance. An additional $71 million FDIC special assessment fee was recognized in 2024.
comparisons.comparison: This disclosure provides granular detail supporting the comparison with Citigroup. Both firms saw operating expenses decline primarily due to the normalization of FDIC special assessment fees and other non-recurring items (Citigroup: restructuring/repositioning; GS: CIE impairments, GreenSky). Citigroup's 2024 expense included a $203 million FDIC assessment, while Goldman Sachs recognized an incremental $71 million fee in 2024 compared to a $529 million fee in 2023. Both also faced offsetting increases in operational costs: Citigroup cited higher volume-related expenses and risk/control initiatives, while Goldman Sachs cited higher compensation and transaction-based expenses.

sentences.text: The decrease was partially offset by higher volume-related expenses, investments in Citi's transformation and other risk and controls initiatives, as well as the costs of the July 2024 Civil Money Penalty Consent Orders entered into with the Federal Reserve Board (FRB) and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC).

Operating expenses, compared with 2023, reflected decreases driven by significantly lower expenses, including impairments ($1.46 billion recognized in 2023), related to commercial real estate in CIEs (largely in depreciation and amortization) and other significant expenses recognized in the prior year, including the write-down of identifiable intangible assets related to GreenSky of $506 million and an impairment of goodwill related to Consumer platforms of $504 million (both in depreciation and amortization), and the FDIC special assessment fee of $529 million (in other expenses).

An incremental expense for the FDIC special assessment fee of $71 million was recognized in 2024, as the FDIC notified banks subject to the special assessment fee of the updated estimated cost to the Deposit Insurance Fund resulting from the closures in 2023 of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank.

comparisons.peer_summary: Noninterest expense was $91.8 billion, up 5%, driven by higher compensation and a $1.0 billion Visa share contribution to the foundation, partially offset by lower FDIC-related expenses due to the timing of special assessments.
comparisons.comparison: While both Citigroup and JPMorgan discuss FDIC special assessments as a key driver of expense variance, the direction and impact were opposite in the aggregate results. Citigroup's 2024 operating expenses decreased 4% ($54.0 billion) because the 2024 FDIC assessment ($203 million) was significantly lower than the prior year's $1.7 billion. In contrast, JPMorgan's noninterest expense increased 5% ($91.8 billion), although this increase was partially offset by lower FDIC-related expense (as the prior year included a $2.9 billion assessment, compared to a $725 million increase in 2024). Thus, while both firms benefited from lower FDIC assessments relative to 2023 peaks, JPMorgan's underlying operational costs (compensation) grew faster than Citigroup's.

sentences.text: Citigroup's operating expenses of $54.0 billion decreased 4% from the prior year.

Excluding the FDIC special assessment ($203 million in 2024 versus approximately $1.7 billion in the prior year), expenses of $53.8 billion decreased 2%, driven by savings related to Citi's organizational simplification and stranded cost reduction, as well as the lower restructuring charges ($259 million in 2024 versus $781 million in the prior year) and repositioning costs.

• Noninterest expense was $91.8 billion, up 5%, driven by higher compensation expense, including higher revenue-related compensation and growth in the number of employees, as well as a $1.0 billion contribution of Visa shares to the JPMorgan Chase Foundation recorded in the second quarter of 2024, partially offset by lower FDIC-related expense, reflecting a $2.9 billion special assessment recognized in the fourth quarter of 2023, compared with a $725 million increase to the FDIC special assessment recognized in the first quarter of 2024.
